Velocities stay local.\n- **OpenMP** runs one thread per GPU assigned to a rank. Each thread drives its device over its sub-block.\n- **CUDA** kernels compute forces with shared-memory tiling. Every body's j-loop is accumulated\n//             in ascending j order (tiled through shared memory), so per-body\n//             results match the sequential reference computation.\n\n#include <mpi.h>\n#include <omp.h>\n#include <cuda_runtime.h>\n\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <chrono>\n#include <cmath>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstdlib>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <vector>\n\n#include \"../common/results_output.hpp\"\n\nconstexpr double SOFTENING = 1e-9;\nconstexpr double DT = 0.01;\nconstexpr int FORCE_BLOCK = 256;  // threads per block; also the shared-memory tile size\n\nstruct Vec3 {\n    double x, y, z;\n    constexpr Vec3(const double x = 0, const double y = 0, const double z = 0) noexcept : x(x), y(y), z(z) {}\n};\n\nstruct Body {\n    Vec3 pos;\n    Vec3 vel;\n};\n\n#define CUDA_CHECK(call)                                                                       \\\n    do {                                                                                       \\\n        cudaError_t err_ = (call);                                                             \\\n        if (err_ != cudaSuccess) {                                                             \\\n            fprintf(stderr, \"CUDA error at %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__,                   \\\n                    cudaGetErrorString(err_));                                                 \\\n            MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1);                                                      \\\n        }                                                                                      \\\n    } while (0)\n\nstruct Range {\n    size_t begin;\n    size_t count;\n};\n\n// Balanced contiguous split of [0, total) into `parts` pieces; returns piece `idx`.\nstatic Range splitRange(size_t total, int parts, int idx) {\n    const size_t b = total * static_cast<size_t>(idx) / static_cast<size_t>(parts);\n    const size_t e = total * static_cast<size_t>(idx + 1) / static_cast<size_t>(parts);\n    return {b, e - b};\n}\n\nvoid randomizeBodies(std::vector<Body>& bodies, unsigned int seed = 42) {\n    for (auto& body : bodies) {\n        body.pos.x = 2.0 * (rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX) - 1.0;\n        body.pos.y = 2.0 * (rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX) - 1.0;\n        body.pos.z = 2.0 * (rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX) - 1.0;\n        body.vel.x = 2.0 * (rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX) - 1.0;\n        body.vel.y = 2.0 * (rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX) - 1.0;\n        body.vel.z = 2.0 * (rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX) - 1.0;\n    }\n}\n\n// Force accumulation for the local body range [first, first + count).\n// pos holds all n bodies (interleaved x,y,z); vel holds the local bodies only.\n// Each thread owns one body i and streams all j = 0..n-1 in order through shared\n// memory, so the summation order matches the sequential reference.\n__global__ void computeForcesKernel(const double* __restrict__ pos, double* __restrict__ vel,\n                                    size_t first, size_t count, size_t n) {\n    __shared__ double sx[FORCE_BLOCK];\n    __shared__ double sy[FORCE_BLOCK];\n    __shared__ double sz[FORCE_BLOCK];\n\n    const size_t li = static_cast<size_t>(blockIdx.x) * FORCE_BLOCK + threadIdx.x;\n    const bool active = li < count;\n\n    double px = 0.0, py = 0.0, pz = 0.0;\n    if (active) {\n        const size_t i = first + li;\n        px = pos[3 * i];\n        py = pos[3 * i + 1];\n        pz = pos[3 * i + 2];\n    }\n\n    double Fx = 0.0, Fy = 0.0, Fz = 0.0;\n    for (size_t base = 0; base < n; base += FORCE_BLOCK) {\n        const size_t j = base + threadIdx.x;\n        if (j < n) {\n            sx[threadIdx.x] = pos[3 * j];\n            sy[threadIdx.x] = pos[3 * j + 1];\n            sz[threadIdx.x] = pos[3 * j + 2];\n        }\n        __syncthreads();\n\n        if (active) {\n            const size_t remaining = n - base;\n            const size_t lim = remaining < static_cast<size_t>(FORCE_BLOCK) ? remaining : static_cast<size_t>(FORCE_BLOCK);\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < lim; ++k) {\n                const double dx = sx[k] - px;\n                const double dy = sy[k] - py;\n                const double dz = sz[k] - pz;\n                const double distSqr = dx * dx + dy * dy + dz * dz + SOFTENING;\n                const double invDist = 1.0 / sqrt(distSqr);\n                const double invDist3 = invDist * invDist * invDist;\n\n                Fx += dx * invDist3;\n                Fy += dy * invDist3;\n                Fz += dz * invDist3;\n            }\n        }\n        __syncthreads();\n    }\n\n    if (active) {\n        vel[3 * li] += DT * Fx;\n        vel[3 * li + 1] += DT * Fy;\n        vel[3 * li + 2] += DT * Fz;\n    }\n}\n\n// Position update for the local body range; writes pos for owned bodies only.\n__global__ void integrateKernel(double* __restrict__ pos, const double* __restrict__ vel,\n                                size_t first, size_t count) {\n    const size_t li = static_cast<size_t>(blockIdx.x) * FORCE_BLOCK + threadIdx.x;\n    if (li >= count) return;\n    const size_t i = first + li;\n    pos[3 * i] += vel[3 * li] * DT;\n    pos[3 * i + 1] += vel[3 * li + 1] * DT;\n    pos[3 * i + 2] += vel[3 * li + 2] * DT;\n}\n\ndouble computeTotalEnergy(const std::vector<Body>& bodies) {\n    double energy = 0.0;\n    const size_t n = bodies.size();\n\n    // Kinetic energy (assuming unit mass)\n    for (const auto& body : bodies) {\n        energy += 0.5 * (body.vel.x * body.vel.x + \n                        body.vel.y * body.vel.y + \n                        body.vel.z * body.vel.z);\n    }\n\n    // Potential energy (assuming unit mass for all bodies)\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {\n        for (size_t j = i + 1; j < n; ++j) {\n            const double dx = bodies[j].pos.x - bodies[i].pos.x;\n            const double dy = bodies[j].pos.y - bodies[i].pos.y;\n            const double dz = bodies[j].pos.z - bodies[i].pos.z;\n            const double dist = std::sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy + dz * dz + SOFTENING);\n            energy -= 1.0 / dist;\n        }\n    }\n\n    return energy;\n}\n\n// Validate that simulation produces finite, reasonable values\nbool validateSimulation(const std::vector<Body>& bodies) {\n    for (const auto& body : bodies) {\n        // Check for std::abs(body.pos.z) > maxPos) {\n            printf(\"Validation failed: body position exceeds reasonable bounds\\n\");\n            return false;\n        }\n        if (std::abs(body.vel.x) > maxVel || std::abs(body.vel.y) > maxVel || std::abs(body.vel.z) > maxVel) {\n            printf(\"Validation failed: body velocity exceeds reasonable bounds\\n\");\n            return false;\n        }\n    }\n    return true;\n}\n\nvoid printUsage(const char* progName) {\n    printf(\"Usage: %s [options]\\n\", progName);\n    printf(\"Options:\\n\");\n    printf(\"  -n <num>     Number of bodies MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &numRanks);\n    const bool root = (rank == 0);\n\n    int numBodies = 1024;\n    int numSteps = 10;\n    bool validate = false;\n    bool printResults = false;\n\n    // {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793090773960,"sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","part":{"id":"prt_17c89c8b8001cCoUW5sw7FsO9i","messageID":"msg_17c89c3bd001d7hXEqRrtJeQNQ","sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","type":"reasoning","text":"I notice np=1 is the outlier that hashes differently while np=2,3,4 match reference. With np=1, R=1 so all 4 GPUs get assigned to a single rank giving nThreads=4, whereas with np=2 or np=3 the devices split across ranks by modulo, changing the thread assignment pattern.\n\nNow I suspect a race condition: hostPos is shared across threads, and each thread does an H2D copy of the full hostPos array at the start while also writing its own D2H slice. If one thread writes its slice back to hostPos while another thread is still reading the full array for its H2D copy, that thread could read post-integration values instead of the correct pre-step positions — a genuine data race that would explain inconsistent results depending on thread/device counts.\n\nThe fix is to split the parallel region into two phases with a barrier in between: first all threads upload and run kernels, then after a barrier (which all threads must reach, including those with zero bodies), they do the D2H writes. This guarantees no thread reads mid-updated positions. I should check that the velocity gather afterward has no similar read/write conflict — it looks fine since nothing reads hostVel in that region. This race likely explains why some N/process counts matched by coincidence and others didn't.\n\n","time":{"start":1793090767032,"end":1793090773877},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}
{"type":"text","timestamp":1793090773961,"sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","part":{"id":"prt_17c89e379001amnWjLxQBZcw6D","messageID":"msg_17c89c3bd001d7hXEqRrtJeQNQ","sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","type":"text","text":"The np=1 mismatch points to a real race in my code. Each thread uploads the full `hostPos` to its GPU at the start of a step, while other threads may already be writing their owned slices back into `hostPos`. A thread can therefore upload a partially updated position array. Results happened to match in some configurations, which is why it looked configuration-dependent. The fix is a barrier between the upload/compute phase and the download phase, executed by every thread.","time":{"start":1793090773881,"end":1793090773895}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793090937002,"sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","part":{"id":"prt_17c8c3313001aXCclQASqwh5O2","messageID":"msg_17c8c2e1e001IXN4VvcVyyaHkx","sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","type":"reasoning","text":"Looking at the scaling numbers: np=1 with 4 GPUs takes 223ms, np=2 takes 217ms, np=4 takes 218ms, but np=8 jumps to 427ms since ranks start sharing GPUs. So within a single node, adding more ranks doesn't help once all 4 GPUs are already in use—the bottleneck is elsewhere, with each GPU handling roughly 4096 bodies per step.\n\nEstimating theoretical FLOPs against the 3090's fp64 rate suggests each step should take only a few milliseconds, yet measured time is ~44ms—so overheads like host-to-device transfers and MPI allgather calls matter, but the kernel itself is likely the real culprit. With only 4096 bodies per GPU split into 16 blocks of 256 threads, the grid is far too small to fill the 3090's 82 SMs, leaving the kernel severely underutilized and effectively latency-bound rather than compute-bound.\n\nI realize each thread runs a long sequential dependency chain accumulating Fx across all 16384 j-bodies, and with so few resident warps per SM there isn't enough parallelism to hide fp64 pipeline latency. Since I can't split the j-loop across threads without breaking bit-exact summation order, I'm considering having each thread handle multiple independent i-bodies interleaved within the same j-loop—this preserves each body's strict accumulation order while giving the warp scheduler more independent chains to interleave for instruction-level parallelism, at the cost of extra registers per thread.\n\nGiven we're already ~44x faster than the reference (223ms vs 9917ms), I should first measure where the remaining time actually goes before adding ILP complexity—profiling kernel time versus H2D/D2H/Allgatherv overhead per step to see if compute or communication dominates at 45ms/step.\n\nComputing rough peak FP64 throughput shows we're running ~17x below theoretical peak, suggesting the kernel is latency-bound from low occupancy (only ~1.6 warps/SM with 4096 threads across 82 SMs). This makes ILP=4 worth trying—giving each thread 4 bodies to process so more work stays in flight per SM, potentially cutting kernel time toward ~10ms, so I'll implement a constexpr for bodies-per-thread.\n\nWriting the strided indexing scheme...\n\n","time":{"start":1793090925331,"end":1793090936983},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

I suspect the heavy register pressure from unrolled accumulators and position arrays is hurting occupancy, and with only 4096 bodies the grid shrinks to just 4 blocks per GPU, cutting parallelism even further.\n\nI'm estimating raw FP64 throughput on these GPUs against what we're actually achieving per step, and it's clear we're latency-bound rather than compute-bound — the theoretical peak would be a few milliseconds but we're seeing 40+. The real fix would be splitting the j-loop across cooperating threads with a reduction, but that breaks the strict sequential summation order needed for bit-exact reproducibility, which is a constraint I imposed myself rather than a hard requirement.\n\nI'm weighing whether reordering floating-point summation is still acceptable under \"equivalent semantics\" — mathematically it's fine and is standard practice in parallelized N-body codes, but I'd rather preserve bitwise-identical per-body results as a strong correctness guarantee, so I'll keep the current design and just document the latency-bound performance.\n\nNow I'm reconsidering the ILP setting — testing ILP=2 against the ILP=1 baseline of 223ms to see which gives better thread occupancy per SM.\n\nILP=4 performed worse, likely because the sqrt/div latency per chain isn't hidden with fewer warps resident, and I suspect register spilling into local memory from the array-based implementation is also hurting things. I want to compile with verbose ptxas output to check for spills and consider avoiding arrays in favor of unrolled scalar registers.\n\n","time":{"start":1793091094698,"end":1793091103135},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793091237177,"sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","part":{"id":"prt_17c90a990001Bb1HqpxdgGEucv","messageID":"msg_17c90a3b7001R0G3Q8qToMSXwe","sessionID":"ses_e837d1792ffeC5f08zumC9JDnV","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm comparing timing: each kernel runs about 41ms for 16384 bodies on a single GPU, which suggests the full problem actually fits in one pass rather than scaling 4x as I'd assumed — so the 214ms total for 5 steps lines up with that single-GPU throughput.\n\nI'm trying to pin down why DP throughput is so low: with 512 warps across 82 SMs at only ~2 FP64 units per SM, each warp's division and square root operations expand into dozens of Newton-iteration instructions, which could plausibly account for the multi-microsecond-per-iteration cost I'm seeing.\n\nThat matches the ~74ms estimate at 1.7GHz, confirming the kernel is FP64-throughput bound given the 3090's 1/64 FP64 rate, not latency-limited. Comparing 1-GPU (16384 bodies) to 4-GPU (4096 each), the smaller per-GPU workload gives roughly 1.56 warps/SM and an estimated 19ms, but the measured 41ms per kernel across 4 devices suggests something else is contributing to the gap.\n\nTrying a latency-bound model with dependent instruction chains gives about 6ms, still well short of 41ms, so that's not quite it either. The oddity is that both the 4096-body and 16384-body per-GPU cases land around 41ms, which points to a per-thread serial chain whose duration doesn't scale with thread count — possibly dominated by slow double-precision division or sqrt operations on the GA102 architecture.\n\nThat's not 2.5µs either. Maybe I should reconsider the clock speed under load and recompute: perhaps each iteration involves around 80 double-precision operations with roughly 8-cycle latency each, giving about 640 cycles total.\n\nConverting that to time at 1.7GHz gives roughly 0.37µs per iteration, so 16384 iterations would be about 6ms -- still off by a factor of 7 from the expected 41ms. Thinking about it more, the division and square root operations in CUDA with strict IEEE precision flags compile to slow-path routines with many dependent instructions and branches, likely around 150 instructions totaling ~1500 cycles, or about 0.9µs per iteration. That scales to roughly 14.5ms across all iterations, and with additional per-tile synchronization overhead, landing near 41ms seems plausible.\n\nI'm now reasoning this is latency-bound on the dependent division/sqrt chain, which means more warps per SM should help hide that latency -- exactly what ILP should address. But testing ILP=4 across 4 GPUs gave a confusing result: 16384 bodies divided by 4 ILP and 4 GPUs works out to 1024 threads or 32 warps per GPU, and if purely latency-bound each warp should run about 4x faster since it has 4 independent chains. Yet the measured time was actually about 3.5x slower (789ms vs 223ms), which doesn't match a latency-bound model -- it looks more throughput-limited, since the total instruction work per SM should stay constant regardless of ILP if bodies per GPU are fixed.\n\nI'm deciding to stop chasing this and accept the current 44x speedup over baseline is good enough, since scaling issues only show up at small per-GPU body counts -- for realistic larger N, per-GPU thread counts should be high enough to fill occupancy. I want to verify this by testing N=65536 across 1 vs 4 GPUs to confirm scaling holds at larger sizes, then finalize. I'm also deciding to drop the ILP/array machinery and revert to the simpler single-body kernel that was already verified bit-exact, since the added complexity isn't worth it.\n\n","time":{"start":1793091217808,"end":1793091237054},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}
